flags.current: A one-year European call on the foreign currency struck at USD 0.5700 trades at USD 0.0325, and its implied volatility is 14.5% per annum.
flags.proposed: Key (c) USD 0.0724 is unchanged. Replace 'its implied volatility is 14.5% per annum' with 'its implied volatility is 23.8% per annum'. In the solution and trap, make the matching change '14.5%' -> '23.8%' (solution: 'consistency with the call's 14.5% is guaranteed'; trap: 'the stated 14.5% implied volatility'). Alternatively keep 14.5% and change the call price to USD 0.0146, but then the put becomes 0.0146+0.547650-0.507714 = 0.0545 and every option has to be rebuilt, so changing the volatility is the cleaner fix.
flags.source_says: Same stem in the PDF (14.5%, call USD 0.0325), where the volatility is described as a red herring
flags.derivation: Garman-Kohlhagen with S=0.55, K=0.57, r=4%, rf=q=8%, T=1, sigma=14.5% gives c = 0.01459, not 0.0325. The volatility that reproduces c = 0.0325 is 23.79%. At that volatility the GK put is 0.07244, which matches the parity answer. The data in the stem therefore contradict each other. The answer is unaffected because parity does not need a volatility. But the solution's claim that 'consistency with the call's 14.5% is guaranteed automatically' is false as stated, and a student who checks the numbers with BSM gets a contradiction.
flags.evidence: PDF p.45 (Q43 stem), p.46 (solution 'The implied volatility of 14.5% is not required ... consistency with the call's 14.5% is guaranteed automatically')

flags.current: II is not necessarily true and is misframed: the statement fixes only the maturity, not the strike, so a comparison between an in-the-money call and an out-of-the-money put is undefined. The defensible statement is that at a given strike an in-the-money call is more expensive than an in-the-money put, which follows from parity rather than from the skew.
flags.proposed: Key (a) is defensible only on the reading 'necessarily true given the skew'. Best fix: reword statement II so it is plainly false and still tests LO 2/3, e.g. 'II. For identical strikes and maturities, the out-of-the-money put carries a higher implied volatility than the in-the-money call.' That is false because put-call parity forces equal implied volatilities. Then change the solution text to: 'II is false: at a common strike and maturity, put-call parity forces the call and the put to share one implied volatility, whatever the skew.' If the stem is kept, at least replace the solution's reasoning with: 'II does not follow from the skew. For a non-dividend-paying stock it holds by no-arbitrage (any ITM call >= ATM call >= ATM put >= any OTM put at the same maturity), and it can fail when the dividend yield exceeds r. So it is not a conclusion licensed by the skew.' Also delete the impossible phrase 'an in-the-money call is more expensive than an in-the-money put' at the same strike.
flags.source_says: PDF gives the same reasoning (II 'undefined'; 'at a GIVEN strike an in-the-money call is more expensive than an in-the-money put') and keys (a) IV only
flags.derivation: The comparison is not undefined. Take an ITM call at strike K1 < S and an OTM put at strike K2 < S, same maturity. Model-free monotonicity in strike gives c(K1) >= c(S) and p(K2) <= p(S). Parity at K = S gives c(S) - p(S) = S e^{-qT} - S e^{-rT}, which is >= 0 when r >= q. So for a non-dividend-paying stock with r >= 0, statement II is necessarily true. The stem does not give a dividend yield (it only says 'large-cap technology stock'). A candidate who assumes no dividends therefore finds I, III false and II, IV true, and no option says 'II and IV only'. Separately, the solution's 'at a given strike an in-the-money call ... than an in-the-money put' is impossible: at one strike, the call and the put cannot both be in the money.
flags.evidence: PDF p.8 (Q7 statement II and solution paragraph on II)

flags.current: optionAnalysis.c: 'Positive serial correlation causes variance to scale faster than linearly in time, raising long-horizon annualised volatility relative to short-horizon. That implies an upward slope, the reverse of what is observed.' Solution: 'Mean reversion is the only one of the four candidates that can produce either slope depending on the current level'
flags.proposed: Key (a) is unchanged. Replace optionAnalysis.c with: 'Serial correlation in returns changes how variance scales with the horizon. Positive autocorrelation raises long-horizon annualised volatility (upward slope) and negative autocorrelation lowers it. It describes returns, not a state-dependent volatility level, so it is not the curriculum explanation for a term structure whose slope depends on where current volatility sits relative to its long-run level.' In the solution, change 'Mean reversion is the only one of the four candidates that can produce either slope depending on the current level' to 'Mean reversion is the candidate whose slope depends on the current level of volatility relative to its long-run level'.
flags.source_says: PDF p.17 has the same optionAnalysis for (c) and the same 'only one of the four candidates' claim
flags.derivation: Var(sum of n returns) = n*sigma^2*[1 + 2*sum_k (1-k/n)*rho_k]. With rho < 0 (negative serial correlation), annualised long-horizon volatility is below short-horizon volatility, which is a downward slope. So serial correlation can produce either slope, depending on its sign. The claim that mean reversion is the only candidate able to produce either slope is false. The (c) rationale silently assumes the correlation is positive, while the option does not state a sign.
flags.evidence: PDF p.17 (Q16 solution and option (c) analysis)
